name: Traditional Square Dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Living Roots of American Square Dancing
This is Traditional Square Dance. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (ZWuQK0WFE44)
Title card: Traditional Square Dance · United States and Canada · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Traditional square dance descends from 18th-century cotillions and 19th-century quadrilles brought by settlers.
It encompasses pre-1950 regional styles across North America, evolving through Northeastern, Southeastern, and Western branches.
on_screen: Map: United States and Canada · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Functioning as community gatherings, survival dances are sponsored by local churches, fire departments, or Granges where attendees mostly know one another.
Revival dances and fun nights open the floor to the public with casual attire and frequent partner changes.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Alliance for Appalachia blockades Obama's Council on Environmental Quality over MTR coal mining (https://archive.org/details/MTRAppalachiaCD992014540p)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced using a limited number of basic movements or 'calls' that enable average dancers to join by assimilation rather than formal lessons.
Figures are executed in set orders or chosen from local repertoires by a prompter or caller, with regional variations appearing primarily in hand and arm positions.
Watch for ladies chain, right and left, Bird in the Cage.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (ZWuQK0WFE44)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Four-couple square formation or large circle where a single couple visits other couples in turn
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Danced almost exclusively to live music derived from Scottish and Irish jigs in 6/8 time and reels in 2/4 time.

Fiddles serve as the primary lead instrument, supported regionally by pianos in New England, banjos and guitars in the South, double basses, accordions in Quebec and Newfoundland, and hammered dulcimers in Michigan.
Listen for the fiddle, piano, banjo, guitar.
The pulse is 6/8 time (jigs) and 2/4 time (reels) at about 130 beats a minute.
Acoustic folk music driven by a lead fiddle playing brisk Scottish and Irish tunes, anchored by a regional rhythm section of piano, banjo, or guitar.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Verified recording — MISSING
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Binary form AABB pattern with 8 measures (16 downbeats) per part

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ted Sannella, Lloyd Shaw, and George Wade.
Classified into Northeastern, Southeastern, and Western types, with documented roots across New England, the southern Appalachian Mountains, the Ozarks, and eastern Canada.
Descended from the 18th-century cotillion and the 19th-century quadrille; serves as the precursor to modern Western square dance.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Traditional Square Dance is parent of modern Western square dance: Modern Western style developed out of a blend of regional traditional square dance styles after 1950.
Traditional Square Dance is sibling of contra dance: Frequently featured alongside traditional squares at public revival dance events.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Traditional Square Dance (United States and Canada). Meter 6/8 time (jigs) and 2/4 time (reels). Tempo about 130 bpm. Rhythm pattern: Binary form AABB pattern with 8 measures (16 downbeats) per part. Instruments: fiddle, piano, banjo, guitar, double bass, accordion, hammered dulcimer. Vocal style: Singing calls where callers substitute dance directions for lyrics during fiddle-tune-structured songs. Mood: lively, energetic, folk, rhythmic. It should sound like this: Acoustic folk music driven by a lead fiddle playing brisk Scottish and Irish tunes, anchored by a regional rhythm section of piano, banjo, or guitar. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
